_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: But according to Rabbi Eliezer, who says “for I say [the se’a that fell is the se’a that arose]”: do we regard them as entirely pure? Yet [the baraita] says they are to be eaten dry, or kneaded [with fruit juice].
gershom:a1.1: And that se’a itself [that was lifted out] is eaten dry, since it is perhaps impure teruma and perhaps non-sacred. And some say “dry” [nikudin] means in crumbs, crumbs of less than an egg-bulk, and he eats all of them in that way, the se’a that arose and the rest.
rashi:a1.2: What is the reason: [that] we do not regard them as fully non-sacred according to the Rabbis, since it was nullified according to Rabbi Eliezer, as he holds “for I say.”
gershom:a2.1: And Ulla says: What is the reason that those non-sacred items are eaten dry, since it is obvious to him [Rabbi Eliezer] that the se’a that fell is the se’a that arose?
rashi:a1.3: A decree lest one bring, etc.: for if we regarded them as entirely pure, there would be concern that when he had a kav of other, impure non-sacred produce, he would bring it and mix it with a kav and a little more of this type, thinking that the first kav is nullified by the majority of this kav-and-a-little-more. But since in this kav-and-a-little-more there is some trace, one part in a hundred, of the impure teruma that fell there and that we now treat as nullified, the first impurity finds the second impurity and is revived out of its status of purity, and joins with it, and they become half and half, which is not nullified. Evidently, impurity that was nullified returns and is revived out of its status of purity.
tosafot:a1.1: He thinks: I will nullify them in the majority. This is puzzling: what would it help? We do not nullify a prohibited item deliberately, and even if one nullified it unwittingly, it is not nullified according to the one who says in Gittin (54b): if they fell and split, whether unwittingly or intentionally, they are not nullified. However, there is an opinion there that unwittingly they are nullified; and perhaps this counts as unwitting, since he thinks it is permitted to nullify.
gershom:a3.1: A decree lest one bring from another place a kav of impure non-sacred produce, and a kav and a little more of this type, from these non-sacred items, and think: this kav of definitely impure non-sacred produce is nullified in the majority of this kav and a little more. And since there is in this kav and a little more that trace — for it is impossible that there not be in them a trace of the se’a of impure teruma that fell into them, even though we said the se’a that fell is the se’a that arose — that type, the kav of impure non-sacred produce, finds its type and is revived out of its nullification in the majority; rather, they join together and are impure.
rashi:a2.1: He said to him: If impurity revives impurity, does purity revive impurity? This is a rhetorical question. That is, how can the water in the pot, which is pure, revive the water in the brine to make it impure?
gershom:a4.1: He said to him: Abaye [said]: brine is not comparable to this, since there it is reasonable that impurity revives impurity, as this trace is impure and this kav of non-sacred produce is impure; therefore they join.
gershom:a5.1: But purity, the pure water in the pot, does it revive impurity? That is, should the pure water in the pot join with the minority of impure water in the brine? Certainly they do not join.
rashi:a3.1: He raised an objection: to Rabbi Yirmeya.
rashi:a3.2: Fit ashes: of the red heifer.
rashi:a3.4: To render impure: the one who touches it, as it is written: “And he who touches the water of sprinkling shall be impure” (Numbers 19:21).
gershom:a6.1: Fit ashes: that is, the ashes of the [red] heifer.
gershom:a7.1: We follow the majority to render impure: if the majority is ashes of the heifer, it imparts impurity, as it is written: “And the person who touches shall be impure until evening” (Numbers 19:22).
rashi:a3.5: And if you say impurity: that is nullified in a majority is not entirely nullified but is considered as if it were present, so that if another impurity is found it joins with it — then granted that this ash does not impart impurity through contact, since its majority is pure and we say he touched the burned ash, which is the majority; but through carrying, at any rate, let it impart impurity, since in any case he lifted and moved the impurity. And we hold that the water of the sin offering and the ashes of the sin offering impart impurity through carrying, in the first chapter of Yoma (14a).
tosafot:a3.1: And if you say impurity is like something present, etc.: From Rashi’s explanation it appears that [Abaye] comes to prove that impurity does not revive impurity, since [nullified] impurity is regarded as not present. But that is not the flow of the Talmud’s discussion, that Abaye should raise a difficulty against himself, since he explained [above] that impurity does revive impurity; and furthermore, it would be difficult for him from the mishna [of teruma that Rav Dimi cited]. Rather, even if impurity is not regarded as present, it is still reasonable that impurity revives impurity, even though it is not regarded as present.
gershom:a8.1: And if you say impurity is like something present and is not nullified, for after it was nullified in a majority it returns and is revived: granted that it does not impart impurity through contact, since once it was mixed we do not know which is which, and perhaps he did not touch that of the heifer;
gershom:a9.1: through carrying, at any rate, let it impart impurity: if he carried all of it, that of the heifer is in it.
gershom:a10.1: Indeed so; but it was stated about it, etc.
rashi:a5.1: A carcass is nullified in a slaughtered animal: a piece of carcass that became mixed with two slaughtered pieces; the carcass is nullified in the majority with regard to imparting impurity, since one kind in a different kind is nullified, and this is a case of one kind in a different kind.
gershom:a11.1: But doesn’t Rav Ḥisda say a carcass is nullified, etc.: as we explained in [chapter] HaKometz, in Menaḥot.
rashi:a5.2: Since it is impossible for a slaughtered animal to become a carcass. And whoever reads “since it is impossible for a carcass to become a slaughtered animal” is in error, since it is possible for a carcass to have the status of a slaughtered animal, so that it imparts no impurity at all: for example, when it rots, its impurity departs from it, as we say below, “What is fit for a ger is called a carcass.” And so it is explained in Menaḥot, in chapter HaKometz Rabba. [The printed daf reads the version Rashi rejects, “impossible for a carcass to become a slaughtered animal,” and the Davidson English’s bold words follow that reading, though its explanation follows Rashi’s.]
tosafot:a5.1: In brief: A carcass is nullified in a slaughtered animal: the Gemara concludes this only for contact, but through carrying it imparts impurity, and necessarily only where the carcass has an olive-bulk in one place, since two half olive-bulks skewered on a stick do not impart impurity through carrying even if carried all day (Ḥullin 124b), unless they are flattened and somewhat joined. Tosafot asks why one who touched all the pieces is pure, and answers that he touched one and then another, never knowing that he touched the impurity, and it is not a doubtful impurity in a private domain since it was nullified in a majority; alternatively, everything melted together, which is like flattened, and this fits even Rabbi Akiva there. They note a slight difficulty, that the same reason that makes it impart impurity through carrying (impurity is regarded as present) should make it impart impurity through contact, and say one can distinguish. They ask why it imparts impurity through carrying for Rabbi Akiva if it cannot come to contact, and answer that here there is a full measure in one place that can be touched, only it is unknown which. Finally they ask why nullification does not help for carrying (he carries an olive-bulk of carcass in the end) yet does help for the prohibition of eating, as shown by Reish Lakish in Zevaḥim (78a), the sciatic nerve in Ḥullin (99b) and the end of Beitza (38a). They answer that in eating each bit is nullified as it is swallowed, like touching one piece after another; and even if carrying impurity here is only rabbinic, the Rabbis decreed it for carrying and not for the prohibition. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:a5.3: And if you say impurity that was nullified is like something present, so that if another impurity is found it returns and is revived, here too: granted that it does not impart impurity through contact, since we do not follow a piece of carcass over two slaughtered pieces [, let it impart impurity through carrying].
gershom:a12.1: We teach it according to Rabbi Ḥiyya, as Rabbi Ḥiyya teaches, etc. And it was stated about it, etc. Let it impart impurity through carrying, since you said impurity is like something present.
rashi:a7.1: It does not impart impurity, neither through contact nor through carrying: and we established above that the Sages touched upon it because of nullification in a majority. And if impurity nullified in a majority is like something present, let it impart impurity through carrying.
gershom:a14.1: And the Talmud resolves: at any rate this is not difficult, for here it is different, because it is decayed impurity, a mass of blood, and therefore it does not impart impurity through carrying.
tosafot:a8.1: This works out well according to bar Padda, etc.: This is puzzling: why did it not raise the difficulty from the case of Rabbi Shimon above (22a), that the offspring disintegrated before it emerged, which is because of nullification in a majority, as Rabbi Yoḥanan explains explicitly in chapter HaMapelet (Nidda 27a)? And above, too, [Rabbi Yoḥanan] said that they said the same thing, implying that Rabbi Shimon’s reason is like that of Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov. And from that case it could have raised the difficulty even according to bar Padda, since with corpse impurity the reason of “fit for a ger” does not apply, and since it does not impart impurity in a tent, evidently [nullified] impurity is regarded as not present. One can answer that it could have deflected this in accordance with Reish Lakish, who disagrees with Rabbi Yoḥanan in chapter HaMapelet (also there) and explains the reason as the confusion of its form: this nonviable fetus in the afterbirth has neither the status of flesh nor the status of bones, as explained in Nidda. Alternatively, [the house is impure] for the reason that a whole corpse is here; therefore according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, when any amount of it was taken away in the blood of birth it is pure, since there is no longer a whole corpse here, while Reish Lakish declares it pure because of the confusion of form. And furthermore, one can say that it could have answered that case in Nidda according to the one who says that something does not overshadow and then overshadow again.
tosafot:a8.2: Severe impurity until for a ger: Rabbi Yoḥanan needed the reason of nullification in a majority above because of his own reasoning, since he holds that both this one and that one are until for a dog; but according to bar Padda [the mass is pure] without the reason of nullification in a majority.
gershom:a15.1: This works out well according to bar Padda, who says severe impurity: that a carcass always imparts impurity through carrying until it is disqualified from being eaten by a ger.
rashi:a8.2: Until for a ger: until it is fit for a ger toshav to eat; but if it rotted and is not fit for a ger, it no longer imparts impurity through carrying. But light impurity, that of contact, imparts impurity until it is disqualified from being eaten by a dog. This works out well: this [mass] is not fit for a ger, and therefore it does not impart impurity through carrying; and through contact also not, since we say regarding the blood of birth that he touched the majority.
tosafot:a8.3: Light impurity until for a dog: concerning light impurity, it is obvious to all of them that it is until for a dog, as we learned (Teharot 8:6): Anything set aside as human food is impure until it is disqualified from being eaten by a dog. Rashi explained that severe impurity is carrying and light impurity is contact, and that the mass of blood does not impart impurity through contact because we say regarding the blood of birth that he touched [the majority]. According to his explanation, bar Padda too holds what Rabbi Yoḥanan said above, that the Sages touched upon it because of nullification in a majority. But this does not seem right. Rather, all impurity of a carcass, whether contact or carrying, is called severe impurity, and that lasts until it is unfit for a ger, since the reason is derived shortly: when it is not fit for a ger it is not called a carcass, and this reason applies to both contact and carrying. And light impurity is the impurity of foods, to count first and second degrees [of impurity]. And we find the terms severe and light impurity used of this in Keritot (21a) and in Nidda, chapter Ba Siman (50b), regarding a young bird that fell into a winepress.
gershom:a16.1: And light impurity: the impurity of foods, with an egg-bulk, always imparts impurity until they are not fit for a dog. And this mass of blood, too, does not impart impurity through carrying for this reason, since it is not fit for a ger, as it is decayed.
gershom:a17.1: But according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, etc.
rashi:b1.1: But this is fit for a dog: and let it impart impurity through carrying. This is difficult for Rabbi Yirmeya.
tosafot:b1.1: Both this one and that one until for a dog: One cannot explain that Rabbi Yoḥanan’s reason is from “And flesh torn in the field you shall not eat; you shall throw it to the dog” (Exodus 22:30), since that verse is needed for [its own matter], feeding to a dog. Rather, one can explain it from what is written: “And the dogs shall eat Jezebel in the portion of Jezreel” (II Kings 9:10): evidently, eating by dogs is called eating. And from this it is proven in the second chapter of Zevaḥim (31a) that one who intends that dogs should eat [the offering] tomorrow renders it piggul.
rashi:b3.1: Rotted from the outset: for example, if its limbs were broken while it was alive and it became wormy. Even though it is fit for a dog, it does not impart impurity through carrying, since it never came under carrying impurity. But if at the outset it was fit for a ger and came under carrying impurity, that does not leave it until it is disqualified for a dog. And if you ask: above, too, why did we leave it as a difficulty? [The Gemara] should have answered that this mass of blood does not impart impurity through carrying because it was rotted from the outset, and even Rabbi Yoḥanan agrees in that case. The answer: it is not rotted from the outset, since it was fit for a ger by virtue of its mother as long as it was in the womb; and so it is established below.
tosafot:b3.1: And the other, to exclude what rotted from the outset, Rabbi Yoḥanan: This is puzzling, for from the discussion in the last chapter of Avoda Zara (67b) it appears that according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, what rotted from the outset does not need a verse to exclude it. In the case where Rabbi Yoḥanan says “its taste and its substance,” and Rav Kahana says, “From all their words we learn that an item imparting a detrimental taste is permitted,” it is established there according to Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Shimon’s reason is explained from this verse, “fit for a ger”; and it says: “And the other,” the one who forbids a detrimental taste, [uses it] to exclude what rotted from the outset; “and the other,” Rabbi Shimon, [holds that] what rotted from the outset needs no verse. One can answer: with regard to the prohibition of eating, certainly no verse is needed, since from the outset it is dust; but with regard to impurity, I might have said that it imparts impurity even though it is not fit to eat, as with a creeping animal, semen and a zav’s discharge.
gershom:b1.1: And the other, Rabbi Yoḥanan: that verse, “You shall not eat of any carcass… to the ger,” serves to exclude where it rotted from the outset, before it became a carcass, so that it was never fit for a ger; that does not impart impurity. But if it was fit for a ger, it always imparts impurity until it is disqualified for a dog.
gershom:b2.1: This too was fit for a ger at the outset by virtue of its mother: for had she not expelled it, and had she been slaughtered and the mass of blood found, it would have been fit for a ger along with the flesh. And since it was fit by virtue of its mother, it is also fit when she expelled it, and by right it should impart impurity, were it not that we say it is nullified in the majority.
rashi:b6.1: Pure brine: for example, one that he brought into contact with water [of a ritual bath]. If any amount of water fell into it, it is impure, as [Rav Naḥman] explains: amei ha’aretz are suspected of mixing half water into their brine, and when any amount falls in, the type finds its type and the water outweighs the brine, and they are impure. And according to the one who does not hold that nullified impurity returns and is revived, it is established as a case where any amount of an am ha’aretz’s water fell into it after the contact.
tosafot:b6.1: We learned there: in tractate Makhshirin (6:3): Rabbi Eliezer [ben Ya’akov] says: Pure brine. Rashi explained: for example, one that he brought into contact with water. And he is right, for here it concerns the brine of amei ha’aretz, as the discussion proves, and the beginning of that mishna. And one cannot say that it is pure without contact because ordinarily the majority is brine, which is not susceptible to impurity, since we said above that they need contact. (And furthermore, it teaches “pure brine” and not “impure brine that was purified through contact.”)
tosafot:b6.2: In brief: Into which any amount of water fell is impure: Tosafot quotes Rashi’s explanation (above) and notes that Rashi wrote “water of an am ha’aretz” rather than “impure water” because the mishna says simply “water.” They ask: according to the one who establishes it as an am ha’aretz’s water falling in after the contact, it is obvious that it is impure, just as at the start, when it needed contact; for it needed contact at the start not because of a majority of brine (a minority of water is nullified) but because perhaps water is the majority, and for that same reason the trace of impure water that fell in after the contact renders the pure water impure again. And had the mishna meant only that an am ha’aretz’s brine needs contact, it should have said so plainly. They answer that the end is unlike the start: at the start one might think the brine does not leave its presumption of impurity merely by relying on the claim that the water is little; but after a contact that makes it pure either way, one might have said that a trace of impure water does not remove it from its presumption of purity merely because water may be the majority. And according to the one who explains the trace as impure water, Rav Naḥman’s inference, “amei ha’aretz are suspected of mixing half water,” means they sometimes mix in half; not that a majority of water would not be impure when a trace fell in (it would), but that if they were accustomed to mix in only a little, a trace of water would not make it impure, since the majority would still be brine. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b3.1: Pure brine, whose majority is not water, which does not need contact: once any amount of water fell into it, it is impure and needs contact.
gershom:b4.1: To mix half water into their brine: and since a trace of water fell into it, it becomes a majority of water and is susceptible to impurity.
gershom:b5.1: And half is not nullified: for we said above that a minority of water is nullified in the majority, but half is not nullified.
rashi:b7.1: Up to half: close to half.
gershom:b6.1: Say: up to half. That is, they mix up to nearly half into their brine, and the trace that fell completes it to half, and it is not nullified.
rashi:b7.2: The impurity of liquids is rabbinic: in the first chapter of Pesaḥim (16a).
gershom:b7.1: And the impurity of liquids is rabbinic: for we expound the verse “And all liquid that may be drunk in any vessel shall be impure” (Leviticus 11:34) thus: what is “shall be impure”? Rendering susceptible. And they impart impurity only by rabbinic law, and the Rabbis decreed only where there is a majority.
rashi:b8.1: MISHNA: One need not be concerned that perhaps it was the offspring of another: such that the next one born would be an uncertain firstborn, as we might say that this animal never gave birth but grew fond of its fellow’s offspring. And if [you object] because it has milk, there is a minority of animals that give milk even though they have not given birth: this we certainly do not say; rather, it is certainly its own offspring, and it is exempt from the firstborn.
gershom:b8.1: One need not be concerned that perhaps it was the offspring of another, this one that it is nursing, and that this one has not yet given birth; rather, it is certainly its own offspring, and it is exempt from the firstborn. And he saw the first-time mothers nursing, and those that are not first-time mothers also nursing: one need not be concerned that perhaps the offspring of this one came to that one, so that all of them would be uncertain firstborns. Rather, those nursing from the first-time mothers are definite firstborns, and the rest are definitely non-sacred.
rashi:b8.2: First-time mothers [mavkirot]: young ones that have only now given birth.
rashi:b8.3: One need not be concerned that perhaps the offspring of this one came to that one: so that we should treat all of them as uncertain firstborns. Rather, certainly those that keep close to the first-time mothers are definite firstborns, and those that keep close to the ones that are not first-time mothers are definitely ordinary.
gershom:b9.1: The halakha in the whole chapter follows the mishna, whether anonymous or stated by a single tanna, where there is no dispute.
gershom:b10.1: To which [mishna] did he say the halakha?
rashi:b10.1: GEMARA: A kav but clean: Rav did not need to teach us [this]. “A kav but clean”: a small amount, since he is mentioned only in a few places; and what it says, “clean,” means that the halakha follows him.
tosafot:b10.1: Rather, to Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov, etc.: And if you say: but the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Shimon regarding the afterbirth above (22a) do disagree [with him, since Rabbi Yoḥanan said the two said the same thing]! And one cannot say that perhaps Rav holds like Reish Lakish, who explains the reason in chapter HaMapelet (Nidda 27b) as the confusion of its form, for that is all the more difficult: if the reason is confusion of form, evidently according to Rabbi Shimon it is not nullified in a majority. One can say: perhaps Rabbi Shimon holds like the one who says severe impurity is until for a ger, according to whom we do not need the reason of nullification in a majority, as we explained above that all carcass impurity, even contact impurity, is called severe impurity. Alternatively, it is not considered a dispute, since they did not disagree with him explicitly about that very matter.
tosafot:b10.2: The teaching of Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov is a kav but clean: Even though there are places where the halakha is ruled according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov, as we find at the beginning of HaDar Im HaNokhri (Eruvin 62b), and Rav himself in chapter HaBa Al Yevimto (Yevamot 60a): there are [cases] where [following him] does not seem reasonable, and therefore it was necessary to rule the halakha.
gershom:b11.1: To Rabbi Eliezer [ben Ya’akov]: this need not be said, since we hold that the teaching of Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov is a kav but clean, and the halakha follows him.
gershom:b12.1: They disagree in a baraita: as is stated below.
rashi:b11.1: Of Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam, and the hair of a blemished firstborn: these are halakhot in the mishna, and they are explained below.
gershom:b13.1: Rav already said this once: below.
rashi:b12.1: It is not a dispute: it is not considered a dispute, and since in the mishna they do not disagree with him, the halakha follows him.
gershom:b14.1: You might have said: when Rav said “the halakha throughout the whole chapter, except for a dispute,” he said it about Rabbi Yosei [ben HaMeshullam], and he said “the whole chapter” because Rabbi Yosei said two halakhot, “one makes a place” and likewise “one who plucks”; therefore he used the expression “the whole chapter”; but in truth the halakha does not follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, since they disagree with him in a baraita. Therefore he said explicitly, “The halakha follows Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam,” to show that what he said, “the halakha throughout the whole chapter,” he said about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, since a dispute in a baraita is not considered a dispute.
